title: Who Taught the Machine?
subtitle: A case history of neural networks, 1943–2026
logline: A machine answers you in fluent sentences, and nobody ever wrote it a rulebook. So who taught it? A teacher follows the case from a lamp in Chicago in 1943 to the present, lighting a candle for each era's certainty and letting it burn exactly as long as people believed it, while the doubters stand at the edge of its light. In the end the culprit is never one person: the case board itself turns out to be shaped like a neural network, with one lantern still dark.

vhs.subject: Computer Science
vhs.tagline: Crack the case of the thinking machine!

staging.note: Staging appendix (script editor, rounds 1, 2 and 6). Fixed geography and recurring-device rules that every shot obeys; shots quote the BOARD MAP and CANDLE-CLOCK RULE text below word for word. Spread into script.json by the assembler.

studyLock.canonical: STUDY LOCK (canonical): every beat in the study, at the case board, on the candle shelf or at the Wall of Forecasts is candleAmber, under the same green-shaded desk lamp, in every era. Era colour enters the study only through practicals: the X-ray chat box glows serverCyan; the window shows the era's sky (dawn gold, rose dusk, snow seen past the glass, never a cooled lamp); a struck match or a candle flame. A shot that crosses between a stage or era location and the study tint-crossfades (crossfadeMood, about 0.6 to 1.2 s, no dip) to candleAmber at the moment the frame reaches the study, board, shelf or Wall, and back again if it leaves; the shot's mood field names its OPENING location only. Two shots in the study that cut together never change tint.
studyLock.examples: ch05-s09b (winter is snow past the window, not a cooled lamp); ch12-s07 (the X-ray box is the only serverCyan); ch03-s05, ch03-s06, ch03-s08, ch04-s08, ch05-s10, ch10-s14 (open in an era location, crossfade to candleAmber on reaching the board, shelf or Wall); ch14 (the study's colour enters only as the shelf's reflection in the window glass).

caseBoard.canonical: BOARD MAP (canonical, from the staging appendix; repeated word for word): the Case Board is a fixed grid of slots laid out as network columns by era, left to right: C1 (1943–1969) the far-left input column, C2 (1969–1997), C3 (2006–2017), C4 (2018–2023), and the output, the glowing chat box, at the far right; the case card WHO TAUGHT IT? hangs in slot K at the board's centre; the suspect cards S1 RULES, S2 KNOWLEDGE and S3 LEARNING hang in the left margin, top to bottom; the founding row F1–F2 runs beneath columns C3 and C4; the question-card thread runs along the board's top edge (slots Q1 to Q4, left to right), a low-chroma oxblood string (emberRed rim mixed about 60% into candleAmber) that glints only where the lamp's pool falls; the Wall of Forecasts hangs to the board's right, its slots W1 to W8 left to right (W1 Turing, W2 chess, W3 Rosenblatt 1961, W4 Florence 2012, W5 Coulom, W6 the 30-to-50-years slip in shadow, W7 Hinton 2017, W8 an empty pin until ch15).

candleClock.canonical: CANDLE-CLOCK RULE (canonical; repeated word for word in every candle shot): every belief candle is cut to the same lit height, 45 scored rings at a pitch of 6 px per ring at L3 (270 px), its flame on the top ring and a small tag at its base giving the year it was lit. It burns down one ring per year the belief is held. The wax that burns away is never lost: it stays above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve, ring-scored and translucent in the haze, so sleeve plus stub is always the full lit height and the SLEEVE's length is the years (16 rings = 96 px; 39 rings = 234 px). The sleeves are the bars of the chart: a longer sleeve means a belief held longer. A candle still lit has a live flame where sleeve meets stub; one put out keeps its sleeve, dark, with a thread of smoke; one that guttered has a frayed rim.
candleClock.definedIn: ch01-s05 (glimpse) and ch02-s04 (first full use); repeated word for word in every candle shot

candles.text: THE BRAIN IS A LOGIC MACHINE
A MACHINE THAT LEARNS WILL SOON SEE, TALK AND THINK
MANY-LAYERED NETS ARE A STERILE EXTENSION
INTELLIGENCE IS KNOWLEDGE, TYPED IN BY HAND

candles.end: out 2023 (Lenat's death), wordless, in the lead-in of ch13-s06; 39 rings = 234 px, the tallest dark sleeve on the shelf; ch15-s08 shows it already dark

candleClock.placement: CANDLE PLACEMENT: every belief candle stands on the one study shelf beneath the case board, ordered by the year on its base tag, left to right; a candle lit late in the film is set into its year's place on the shelf (so the 1999 expert-features candle, lit in ch08-s01, stands left of the 2006 warm-up candle lit in ch07-s02, and the 1997 read-in-order candle, lit in ch10-s01, stands left of both). The China-race candles of chapter 14 (COMPUTE IS THE CHOKEPOINT, CHINA IS A YEAR OR TWO BEHIND, the match, THE GAP IS MONTHS, NOT YEARS) stand at the shelf's right end, by the study window; chapter 14 shows them only as a reflection in that window over the strait (opened in ch13-s06), never on the jetty; ch15-s08 sees them directly.
candleClock.finaleChart: ch15-s08 reads the shelf as a bar chart in wax: sleeves of every length with no trend by decade. Tallest dark bar: Cyc 39; then read-in-order 20, sterile 17, logic 16, fiddly-nets about 16 (frayed), expert stencils 13, learning-machine about 7 (frayed), knowledge about 7, warm-up about 5 (frayed), Go 2, China one-to-three about 2, the match flat. Still lit at the right end as of October 2026: learned features (2012), scale (2020, trimmed), compute chokepoint (2022, contested), smarter-than-human AI may be years away and dangerous (2023), the gap is months, not years (2025, contested).

staging.xrayColumn: Defined in ch02-s08: the chat box as a translucent column of seven faint bands, bottom to top: 1 threshold lanterns (1943), 2 adjustable knobs (1958), 3 hidden layers and a backward arrow (1986), 4 furnaces and a sea of text (2012), 5 threads (2017), 6 type sorts (2018), 7 shears (2022); a seam between bands 3 and 4 that never lights (the hand-cut stencils). Each X-ray beat lights exactly one new band; ch12-s07 lights them all.
staging.hands: cast.json 'narrator-hands': the detective's two steady, cuffed tweed forearms (a mid-life teacher's, forties or fifties; the signet ring kept; never aged or weathered) from a fixed lamp-side entry at lower right (L5); six actions only: pin, unpin/drop, strike match/light, fold into the file, stamp, hold up.
staging.accentBudget: One saturated accent per shot, motivated by a practical light. The question thread is low-chroma oxblood (see questionThread). Full saturated red is used once only: the STATUS: OPEN stamp in ch15-s09.
staging.transitions: Signature transitions (lampChange, iris, inkBleed, fadeBlack) only for real mood changes, chapter breaks or the push-into-the-flame cue; same-mood changes are plain cuts, crossfades or occluder wipes. Wherever a lampChange stays, the incoming leadIn and the outgoing holdAfter are at least 1.6 s (iris 1.2, inkBleed 1.1).
staging.textRule: Besides the date/place stamp and name cards, at most two text items per shot. Two exceptions, each counting as ONE item: DISSENT TAGS (the short attributed tags that ring a contested candle, as in ch14-s04b and ch14-s07), up to three per shot, about 48 characters or fewer each, cued at least 1 s apart; and a TWO-ACCOUNTS label (both sides of one disputed event on a single card, at equal size, as in ch11-s08). A quote shown but not spoken gets a music-only window of at least (characters / 12 + 1.5) s. Quotes over about 160 characters are cut to the fragment the shot needs; the rest move to the end-credits sources card (creditsSources). DATE AND PLACE STAMPS use the era's face: Special Elite typewriter for 1943 to the end of the 1970s, VT323 phosphor type for the 1980s, IBM Plex Mono from 1989 on; chapter index tabs are always Special Elite.

creditsSources.text: We sort of quit science for a while to watch the machine. — Marvin Minsky, recalling 1951
“…the views of the loyal opposition…” — Frank Rosenblatt, 1961
samples a different architecture, but all these architectures share weights — Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton, 2012
If you have a thousand words, you have to wait for a thousand cycles. — Illia Polosukhin, 2024
the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms — Vaswani et al., 2017
the dot products grow large in magnitude — Vaswani et al., 2017
almost 50,000 workers from 167 countries — Fei‑Fei Li, 2015, of ImageNet's labellers

I believe that in about fifty years' time it will be possible to programme computers, with a storage capacity of about 10⁹, to make them play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator will not have more than 70 per cent. chance of making the right identification after five minutes of questioning. — Alan M. Turing, 1950
Not Hebb's words: 'fire together, wire together' is a 1992 paraphrase.
There is no Nobel prize for computer science so this is an interesting way of creating one, but it does seem a bit of a stretch. — Dame Wendy Hall, 8 October 2024
You see, we've never had to deal with things more intelligent than ourselves before. — Geoffrey Hinton, December 2024
Current frontier systems are already showing signs of self-preservation and deceptive behaviours — Yoshua Bengio, 3 June 2025
So it's back to the age of research again, just with big computers. — Ilya Sutskever, 25 November 2025
Even if I become the number one, there is an entity that cannot be defeated. — Lee Sedol, to Yonhap, November 2019
Money has never been the problem for us; bans on shipments of advanced chips are the problem. — Liang Wenfeng, founder of DeepSeek, July 2024 (ChinaTalk translation)
…trained using 900 queries in less than an hour. — Christiano et al., 2017 (a simulated Hopper robot learned backflips from human choices)
2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry: half to David Baker, half jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper (DeepMind), for protein structure prediction
I have never claimed that I invented backpropagation. David Rumelhart invented it independently long after people in other fields had invented it. — Geoffrey Hinton, April 2020
ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, 2010: 1.2 million training photos, 1,000 categories
Timnit Gebru left Google in December 2020: she says she was fired; Google says it accepted her resignation.

In the NYT today, Cade Metz implies that I left Google so that I could criticize Google. Actually, I left so that I could talk about the dangers of AI without considering how this impacts Google. Google has acted very responsibly. — Geoffrey Hinton, 1 May 2023 (tweet, as widely reproduced)
Gender Shades (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018): commercial gender classifiers erred on up to 34.7% of darker-skinned women and at most 0.8% of lighter-skinned men.
Equal contribution. Listing order is random. — Vaswani et al., 2017 (the paper was submitted at the NIPS deadline, 19 May 2017)
I have never met anyone who remembered hearing the talk. — John J. Hopfield, recalling his Versailles talk of summer 1981

Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war. — Statement on AI Risk (Center for AI Safety), 30 May 2023
Hinton's company chose Google; the deal was announced in March 2013 (as reported by Cade Metz).
AlexNet also used overlapping max-pooling: 3 × 3 windows stepped two at a time, keeping each window's brightest value (Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton, 2012).
Amazon Mechanical Turk, the marketplace where ImageNet's labellers worked, closed on 30 September 2026.
29 September 2026: the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six tech leaders; voluntary, with no penalties (Microsoft and Amazon did not sign).

kitWork.note: KIT WORK (script editor, rounds 3, 4 and 8): every kit extension or new prop the script depends on that docs/film/kit-catalog.md does not yet provide (none of these is in the catalogue as of round 8). Each is a BLOCKING dependency for film-shots unless it names a fallback: build it (with a gallery entry and a contact-sheet check) before authoring any shot listed against it. Shots that say 'KIT DEPENDENCY' or 'KIT WORK' refer to this list. BUILD ORDER (round 8): items are listed in build order ('order'), the film's SPINE first: (1) the one-study state table (caseBoard, candleShelf, wallOfForecasts, xrayColumn and the derived studyState module), (2) the narratorHands rig, (3) the beliefCandle prop; together they gate about half the film's shots. Then everything else by shot count ('shotCount'). SPINE GATE: before ANY shot is authored, render ONE contact sheet of the study state table at five points in the film, ch01-s05, ch05-s10, ch08-s14, ch12-s07 and ch15-s08 (board slots, shelf candles with their sleeves and stubs, Wall slips and X-ray bands as studyState returns them at each shot, hands at rest at the L5 entry), and check it against BOARD MAP, CANDLE-CLOCK RULE, the Wall of Forecasts table and the X-ray column; fix the state table, not the shots. hallOfMirrors (2 shots) has a non-blocking fallback (see its entry).

studyCameras.canonical: STUDY CAMERAS (canonical): every study visit uses the camera of the device it visits, so no two kinds of visit look alike. BOARD: always frontal and medium on the Case Board, the lamp's pool on the board; pins, unpins and stamps are 1–2 s inserts, never a held wide. SHELF: always a low macro along the candle rings at shelf height, shallow depth of field, haze between candles; candles are read as sleeves and stubs, never from above. WALL: always a slow lateral truck along the Wall of Forecasts from the lamp outward (W1 toward W8), slips in passing focus. FILE: always top-down on the desk (the manila file, the slip folded in, the flap closed). X-RAY: the chat box framed square-on as a plate, the room falling away behind its serverCyan glow. THE FULL WIDE (board, shelf and Wall in one frame) is reserved for exactly three moments: ch01-s05, ch12-s07 and ch15-s08.
studyCameras.board: frontal, medium; inserts of 1–2 s for pins
studyCameras.shelf: low macro along the rings; shallow focus; haze between candles

runtime.note: RUNTIME BUDGET (script editor, round 5 wrap-up). Brief: 30–35 min, target 32 min ≈ 3,040 narration words. Gate: generator/film/script.mjs assemble at 140 wpm (house pace; voice.json wpm overrides once cast) must be at or under 35.2 min. Numeric hold, lead-in and pause lengths quoted inside shot visual text (e.g. "holdAfter 5.5 s", "about 10 seconds") are superseded by the shot fields and the locked clock (timeline.json); shot authors time to the clock.
runtime.timingModel: leadIn + line (words / wpm) + pauseAfter … + holdAfter, max with minDuration, summed over all shots; on-screen text needs characters / 12 + 1.5 s from its beat to the end of its shot
runtime.round5: Cut from 38.4 to about 35.0 min at 140 wpm with every on-screen text item at full reading time (0 reading-time warnings). Words: the film-wide notes' cuts plus ear-pass trims (L1019, L1509, L0512 quote shortened to its first sentence with the rest in creditsSources, L0613/L0614, L0615, L0218, L0307, L0401, L0410, L0522, L0302, L0821, L0114, L1401, L1502); a few ear-pass additions (L0210 sets up the rim aloud, L0807 says 'nine holes', L0907 names Lee Sedol as the opponent, L1104 reminds who said 'practically nothing', L1312 names the three laureates). Air: every non-protected shot's holdAfter set to exactly what its text and its last beat need (0.5 s floor after the last line, 2 s at chapter ends); pauses 0.6–1.5 s cut by 20%; long pauses and lead-ins trimmed; post-narration beat offsets compressed by 30%; labels cued earlier, mid-line, where they name what is being said; long attributions and sourcing caveats moved to creditsSources. Protected: the opening, the deaths in ch04, the transformer reveal, the last narrated shot, the title and credits cards.
runtime.gate: Gate: script.mjs assemble at the locked voice pace (voice.json wpm 143.5) under the 35.2 min ceiling, and at or under 33.6 min (story editor, round 7; round 8 measured 34.7 min after the reviewers' requested additions: see round8). foundingGrammar.canonical: FOUNDING GRAMMAR (canonical, every lab): flat even light, no office, no spotlight, no faces, no hero framing; a typewritten announcement pinned in the founding row (F1 OpenAI, 11 December 2015, ch09-s04; F2 Anthropic, founded January 2021, announced 28 May 2021, ch12-s03), same height and size, no name card under the pin (founders are named only in the narration); a warm and a cold hand-lantern hanging from the same nail; one plain ledger page in IBM Plex Mono for the lab's money. The lantern MEANINGS never change from lab to lab: the WARM lantern is always the promise the lab names, the COLD lantern is always the danger the lab names. OpenAI: warm on 'benefit', cold on 'damage'. Anthropic: cold on 'safety' (the risk its name answers, as OpenAI's 'damage'), warm on 'research'. The order of swings may differ; the meanings may not.
